justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift over time, starting near 62.9 and rising gradually to 63.8 over the one-month horizon. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is anchored heavily by recent observed values and short-term momentum, assuming little meaningful change overnight. For the one-week estimate, I incorporated a slight positive bias reflecting whatever underlying trend or mean-reversion dynamic was present in the data, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for modest directional movement to accumulate. By the one-month mark, the point estimate edges higher still, driven by the assumption that the same gentle trend continues, though the magnitude of any single-period move compounds across more time steps.

The confidence interval widths grow systematically with the forecast horizon, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty accumulates over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 2.8 units, consistent with the relatively predictable short-run behavior of most financial or economic series. By one week, the interval widens to roughly 5.4 units, capturing the increased possibility of unexpected news, sentiment shifts, or data releases. At one month, the interval nearly doubles again to about 10.6 units, reflecting the many possible paths the variable could take across dozens of trading or calendar days, including regime changes in volatility or correlation structure that are hard to anticipate from a snapshot of current conditions.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic announcements, geopolitical shocks, or liquidity events that compress or spike the underlying variable far beyond its recent range. At the one-day horizon, a surprise policy decision or major data release could easily breach the narrow bounds I set. Over a month, a structural break — such as a shift in central bank guidance, a credit event, or an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tension — could drive the variable well outside the 58.5 to 69.1 range. My intervals implicitly assume a relatively stable volatility environment, so any sustained pickup in realized volatility would make those bounds too tight in retrospect.
